failure_modes: Co-eluting non-EV complexes (lipoproteins, aggregates, ribonucleoproteins) bind capture reagents and co-fractionate with particle peaks, causing false co-localization of spike-in, marker signal, and activity despite no intact-EV causal role (confounding by co-elution).

Spike-in tracer behaves differently from endogenous EVs (different density, surface chemistry, or capture-epitope presentation) so spike-in recovery falsely validates fraction recovery while endogenous EVs are lost (misleading positive control).

Capture reagents or buffers interact with secretome components or spike-in tracer (binding/sequestration or epitope masking), producing assay incompatibility that yields false pass/fail calls unless orthogonal reagents/conditions are tested (assay artifact).

Detergent+protease treatments alter the in vitro assay readout (e.g., residual detergent affecting cell responses or protease digest of soluble cytokine-binding factors) so loss of activity after disruption reflects assay interference, not membrane-protected cargo loss (false attribution).

Insufficient material yield from bounded fractions prevents replicate fraction-level functional testing or forces pooling that masks lot-to-lot variability, making the qualitative replication claim unmeasurable.

The in vitro microglia assay has limited dynamic range or is sensitive to matrix effects from fraction eluates (e.g., residual media components), producing variable readouts that obscure true co-localization patterns (low assay robustness).

Even if EV-associated bioactivity is correctly identified in vitro, intranasal delivery barriers and species-specific biodistribution (strong nasal retention, negligible brain uptake in larger species) may render the EV-centric candidate non-translatable for the intended route, misleading program direction (false external validity).

Protease/detergent controls fail (incomplete inactivation, residual activity, or off-target degradation) producing ambiguous protection assay outcomes and irreproducible pass/fail calls (control failure).
strongest_objection: The single strongest bounded risk is misattribution of biological activity to intact, membrane-protected EVs because co-eluting non-vesicular complexes (protein aggregates, lipoproteins, ribonucleoprotein complexes, or other secretome components) or assay-interfering excipients will bind capture reagents and/or carry the functional signal; spike-in recovery or detergent/protease readouts can be confounded by buffer incompatibility, reagent cross-reactivity, or protease/detergent effects on assay biology, producing a reproducible but false ‘‘protected EV activity’’ signature that drives an incorrect EV-centric development path.
